summary: This unit teaches you to lead innovation and continuous improvement in a public body. You will learn the difference between the two and the types of innovation, how to build a culture where ideas are welcome, how to collect, score and choose ideas, how to write a business case and run a pilot, and how to scale what works. You will also learn the main improvement methods (PDCA, Lean, Six Sigma, benchmarking), how to measure results, and how to capture lessons and keep the gains.

blocks.p: This unit is part of the Business Administration (Management) Level 5 qualification. Citizens expect public services to be faster, simpler and more reliable every year, while budgets stay tight. Managers meet this expectation in two ways: by **innovation**, which brings in new ideas, and by **continuous improvement**, which keeps refining the way things are done today. A good manager needs both, and needs to know how to run them with care for public money, the law and fairness to every citizen.

head: What you must be able to do
What this means in a public body
rows: Tell them apart, name the types of innovation and link them to the organisation's strategy and risk appetite.
Lead openly, accept that trials can fail, recognise staff, remove barriers, set up idea systems and use outside partners.
Collect ideas, score them against agreed criteria, calculate weighted scores and use stage gates.
Estimate costs, benefits, payback and risks, and present them to a committee or board.
Design a pilot with a baseline and measures, evaluate it honestly, and decide whether to scale, change or stop.
Apply PDCA, Lean, Six Sigma, total quality management and benchmarking to real processes.
Follow procurement rules, the data protection law and fair-access duties; consult staff affected.
Use results, quality, staff and learning indicators; record lessons; write new methods into procedures.

ul: A **multiple-choice theory paper** with workplace scenarios and short calculations (weighted scores, percentage change, payback).
A **written paper** with short answers (exact terms and sums) and longer answers on culture, selecting ideas, piloting, improvement methods and sustaining change.
**Practical group tasks**: designing an innovation and improvement framework for a made-up agency, and presenting a business case and pilot plan to a role-play innovation committee.

blocks.note: Short-answer questions ask for exact terms: radical innovation, laggards, DMAIC, quality management system, pilot, benchmarking, prototype, open innovation, stage-gate, risk appetite, design thinking and scaling up. They also ask for sums such as payback in months and cost per application. Learn them from the Revision section.
blocks.label: Tip

head: Point
Innovation
Continuous improvement
rows: Bringing in something **new**: a new service, method or way of organising
**Refining** what exists, in many small steps, all the time
Can be small or large, sometimes a leap
Lower: changes are tested and small
Anyone, often with outside input and special projects
Everyone, as part of their daily work
A shared service unit that handles human resource work for several ministries
The records office trims the number of signatures needed on a standard form

blocks.p: A public body needs both. Improvement keeps today's services good and cheap; innovation prepares for tomorrow's needs and makes big gains where small refinements cannot.

head: Type
What it is
Example
rows: A new or much better service for citizens
A mobile unit that takes registration services to rural communities
A new way of delivering the service
Online application and payment of a licence
A new way of structuring work, teams or responsibilities
One shared service unit handling payroll for five ministries
A new way to reach and involve people
Text-message reminders for appointments or payment dates

head: Degree
Meaning
Example
rows: A small improvement to an existing process or service
Adding a payment link to existing tax notices
A large change that replaces the old way of working entirely
Moving a whole licensing service from paper counters to a single online system
A new approach that starts small, serves people poorly served so far, and then changes the field
Low-cost tele-health consultations that begin with remote communities

ul: Citizens expect speed, convenience and online services.
Budgets are tight, so the same or more must be done with less.
Problems are complex and cut across ministries, such as youth unemployment, climate risk and health.
Technology, such as digital payments and data, creates new options.
Hurricanes, pandemics and other shocks show the need to adapt quickly.

blocks.p: An innovation programme should begin from the organisation's **strategic goals and corporate plan**. Ask first: which goals are we trying to reach and where are the biggest gaps? Innovation for its own sake, or a pet project of one director, wastes money. A programme linked to goals also helps to win the support of the board, the ministry and the staff.

**Risk appetite** is the amount and type of risk a board is willing to accept in pursuit of its objectives. A public body may have a very low appetite for risk to public safety, but a higher appetite for trying new ways of serving customers online. The appetite tells managers **where bolder trials are welcome and where they are not**. A committee that funds only small, safe projects every year may be too cautious and miss large gains; one that funds big, risky projects without testing wastes public money.

blocks.note: In the public sector, the test for a new idea is not only "will it save money?" It is also "is it lawful, fair to all citizens, safe, and good value for public funds?"
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.p: The main role of a senior manager in an organisation-wide improvement programme is to **set direction, give resources and remove barriers**. Staff watch what leaders do, not what they say.

ul: **Say it and show it**: explain why innovation matters and join in.
**Accept that trials can fail**: say openly that planned trials may fail and will be learned from. Staff who fear blame do not suggest ideas.
**Give time and money**: a small innovation fund with clear rules helps agencies that say they have no spare budget.
**Give permission**: authority to test new things within agreed limits.
**Recognise**: thank people quickly and show what changed as a result.
**Remove barriers**: for example, replace five separate sign-offs with one.

blocks.h: Common barriers and ways round them

head: Barrier
Sign
What to do
rows: "If it fails, you get the blame"
Leaders state that planned trials may fail; review what was learned, not who is at fault
Simplify: a fast route for small tests; clear delegation of authority
Small innovation fund; protected time for project work
Two units improve the same process without knowing about each other
Share plans; bring units together under one coordinated project
Review rules; ask for approval for pilots under controls
No one knows how to run a pilot or test
Train staff in methods; form a community of practice
Reply quickly, publish what happened to every idea

ul: An **idea system** (online or a suggestion box) open to all staff, with a named person who replies within a fixed time and gives feedback on every idea.
**Frontline staff** meet the public every day and know where the process fails. Parish offices across the island should be able to send ideas as easily as headquarters.
**Customers and citizens**: surveys, complaints analysis, focus groups.
**Staff teams and challenges**: short innovation challenges on a problem such as queues.

head: Approach
What it is
Example
rows: Drawing on ideas from **outside** the organisation, such as universities, firms and citizens
An agency asks a university, local software firms and the public for ways to cut queues
Designing a service **with** the people who use it
Inviting customers, including older people from rural areas, to help redesign a complaints service
Comparing your processes and results with the best similar organisations, and learning from them
A municipal corporation finds that another approves building plans in half the time and studies how
A group of people in different units who meet to share methods and problems
Improvement project leads from several ministries meeting online each month

blocks.p: When an officer develops a new tool during work time, using the agency's equipment, the **agency** normally owns it. Staff should be told this clearly in policy, and credited and thanked for their ideas. Agreements with universities or firms should say who owns and may use anything developed.

The way of recognising staff most likely to keep ideas coming is **thanking people promptly and showing what changed**. A letter of thanks, a mention at a staff meeting, an invitation to present to the board, or support to lead the next project all cost little. A reward that arrives a year later, or never, kills ideas.

blocks.note: Staff should be consulted early about any change to their working hours, duties or conditions. Involve the staff affected and their union or association before the plan is fixed. Changes forced on people without notice cause resistance and may break agreements or employment law.
blocks.label: Safety

sections.title: Choosing ideas and making the business case

flow: **Collect** ideas from everywhere and record them in one place
**Screen**: remove those that are against the law, outside the mandate or already tried
**Score** the rest against agreed criteria (impact, cost, ease, risk, fit with goals)
**Develop** the best into a business case, with a prototype if useful
**Pilot** a small version in one or two places, with measures
**Decide**: scale up, change or stop
**Embed** the new way and share the lessons

blocks.p: **Design thinking** is a human-centred approach: start by understanding the people who use the service, then define the problem, generate many ideas, build a quick **prototype** (an early simple model that users can try) and test it. It prevents spending money on something that nobody needs.

When an innovation committee gets 60 ideas and can fund five, it needs a fair way to choose. **Score each idea against agreed criteria, with weights** that show their importance. Multiply each score by its weight and add up. The weights must total 100%.
**Worked example.** Criteria and weights: impact 40%, cost 35%, ease 25%. Scores are out of 10.

Idea B has the highest score. Check the sums twice. For cost, a **high score means low cost** (the cheaper the idea, the more points), so that a higher total is always better. The score helps the committee; it does not replace judgement. A committee may still choose a bolder, lower-scoring idea for a pilot if it fits the risk appetite.

In a **stage-gate** process, an innovation passes through set stages (idea, business case, pilot, rollout). Between stages there is a **gate**, at which a decision is made to **go on, change or stop**. Gates save money by stopping weak ideas early, and give the board control.
Before asking for money to roll out a new service, a director prepares a **business case**. It should show:

ul: the **problem** and why it matters, linked to the strategic goals;
the **options** considered, including doing nothing;
the **costs**: set-up, running, training, risks;
the **benefits**: money saved, time saved, quality, citizens reached, staff satisfaction;
the **risks** and how they will be managed;
the **legal and procurement** points;
the **plan**, timeline and who is responsible;
how success will be **measured**.

head: Measure
How to work it
Example
rows: Cost ÷ saving per year (or per month)
Time to issue a permit falls from 15 days to 9 days: (15 − 9) ÷ 15 × 100 = **40%**
Ideas put into practice ÷ ideas received × 100

blocks.note: Payback ignores benefits after the payback date and the value of money over time. It is a quick test, not the whole case. A project that also reaches rural citizens or improves safety may be worth more than its savings show, so judge on service quality and public value as well as cost.
blocks.label: Remember

ul: **Procurement:** even a quick test that uses public money with a supplier the agency has not used before must follow the **procurement rules for public bodies**.
**Data protection:** an idea that shares citizens' personal data between agencies must be checked against the data protection law before it goes ahead: what is shared, why, and how it is kept secure.
**Fair access:** a service that moves fully online must still be open and fair to people without the internet, a smartphone or the skills to use it.
**Staff:** consult those affected.

blocks.p: A **pilot** is a small-scale trial of a new idea in one place before it is rolled out across the organisation. It tests the idea, finds problems and gives evidence, **at low risk**.

flow: **Agree** with the sponsor the measures and targets that will judge success, **before** the pilot starts
**Set a baseline**: measure the current situation (for example the missed-appointment rate) before changing anything
**Choose the sites** (and, if possible, a comparison site that is not changed)
**Run** the pilot for long enough to see real results (not only the first excitement)
**Collect** data and user and staff views during the pilot
**Evaluate**: did it work, why, for whom, at what cost, with what side effects?
**Decide**: scale up, adapt and run again, or stop

blocks.p: **Example.** A health region tests text reminders for clinic appointments at two clinics. Before the pilot, 120 of 500 appointments (24%) were missed. In the pilot, 75 of 500 (15%) were missed. The change is (24 − 15) ÷ 24 × 100 = **37.5%** fewer missed appointments, or 45 fewer missed appointments in 500.

ul: Compare with the **baseline**, not with hopes.
Look for **other causes**: did something else change, such as the season, a campaign or a holiday?
Count the **costs**, including staff time.
Ask the **users** and the **staff**: did it work for older people, people without phones, people with disabilities?
Check **unintended effects**: did the change create new problems for another unit?

Treat a **failed pilot as learning**: a trial that is stopped after three months because few people use it has told you something valuable, and the lesson should be recorded. It is a reason to adjust or stop, not to blame the team.

blocks.p: **Scaling up** extends a proven innovation from the pilot site to the whole organisation. Before scaling up, confirm that:

ul: the **results are real** and would hold elsewhere (the pilot worked in Portland: will it work in St Elizabeth, where roads, phone coverage and population differ?);
there is **funding** for the full running costs;
there are **trained staff** and equipment;
**legal, procurement and data** issues are solved;
the **risks** have been reviewed;
there is a **communication and change plan**.

blocks.h: Adoption: how people take up new ideas

blocks.p: The **diffusion of innovations** model shows that people adopt new ideas at different speeds. Plan for each group.

head: Group
Description
What helps
rows: Few; keen to try anything new
Respected opinion leaders who try new things early and help colleagues
Use them as champions and trainers
Adopt once they see it works
Cautious; adopt when most others have
Last to adopt; prefer the old way
Respect their concerns; provide help; set a clear date for the old way to end

ul: Explain **why**: link it to services and goals.
Brief **all** staff: briefings, early success stories and open forums are the best approach for an organisation-wide programme.
Train people **before** the change.
Listen and fix problems quickly.
Do not leave it to chance: name a leader and a timetable.

flow: **Plan**: find the problem, study the data, decide the change and the measure
**Do**: try the change on a small scale
**Check**: compare the results with the measure
**Act**: adopt the change if it worked, or change the plan, then start again

blocks.p: PDCA is the engine of continuous improvement. Each turn teaches something. The Japanese word **kaizen** means continuous improvement by everyone, in small steps.

blocks.h: Process mapping and finding the cause

ul: **Map the process** step by step with the people who do it, showing how long each step takes and how long the work waits between steps.
**Ask "why?" five times** to get from a symptom to a root cause.
**Use data**: counts of errors, times, complaints; show them in a chart.
Use a **cause-and-effect (fishbone) diagram** to list possible causes under headings such as people, method, equipment and information.
**Fix the cause**, not the symptom.

blocks.p: **Lean** is an approach that focuses on removing **waste**: anything that uses time, money or effort without adding value for the citizen. A passport office that maps its process and finds that applications wait in trays for days between steps that take minutes has found waste in the form of **waiting**.

head: Waste
Public-office example
rows: Files waiting in a tray between steps
Four signatures on a form that needs one
Applications returned because of mistakes in the form
Officers walking between buildings to collect a stamp
Printing reports that no one reads

blocks.p: **Six Sigma** uses data to reduce errors and variation. Its improvement cycle is **DMAIC**:

flow: **Define** the problem, the customer and the goal
**Measure** how the process performs now
**Analyse** the data to find the root causes
**Improve**: test and put in the solution
**Control**: keep the gain with standards, checks and monitoring

head: Point
Lean
Six Sigma
rows: Remove waste and speed up flow
"Where does the work wait or repeat?"
Best fit in a public body
Long processing times, queues, hand-offs between units
Pension calculations, payments and records where accuracy matters

blocks.note: The two are often combined ("Lean Six Sigma"): use Lean to speed the flow, then Six Sigma to bring errors down. Choose the method that suits the problem, rather than a favourite.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.p: **Total quality management** is an approach in which **every department and every employee works to improve quality all the time, with the customer at the centre**. It is organisation-wide: leaders commit, staff are trained, customers' needs are measured and data guide decisions. A public hospital that works this way puts the patient at the centre of every process.

A **quality management system (QMS)** is the documented set of policies, processes and responsibilities an organisation uses to manage the quality of its services. Some bodies seek outside **certification** that their system meets an international standard. The certificate shows that the quality system **has been audited as meeting** the standard. It does not guarantee that every service is perfect.

**Benchmarking** compares your processes and results with the best similar organisations, at home or abroad, in order to learn from them. Study how they work, then **adapt** what fits your own law, size and culture; do not copy without thinking.

ul: **Standardise**: write the new method into procedures, checklists and training, so that it does not depend on one person. When the manager who led a successful improvement moves to another post, this is what keeps the gain.
**Monitor**: keep measuring, to catch slipping.
**Train** new staff in the new way.
**Review again**: when results level off, continuous improvement says to look for the next gain.

blocks.p: A programme should be judged on **results**, not only on activity. Use a balanced set of indicators.

head: Area
Examples of indicators
rows: Number of ideas received; **share of ideas put into use** (implementation rate); time from idea to decision
Waiting time, error rate, cost per transaction, citizen satisfaction, access for rural and vulnerable people
Savings, payback, cost per unit, benefits against budget
Staff engagement survey results, staff who have taken part in improvement projects, training done
Lessons recorded and shared, pilots completed, projects scaled up or stopped on evidence

blocks.p: Judge innovation on **service quality, staff engagement and learning as well as cost savings**, because cost alone misses the gains for citizens, staff and the organisation's learning.

A year after rolling out a new service, review first **whether the expected benefits were achieved**. Compare with the business case and the baseline; find out why any gap exists; decide what to adjust.

An agency ran a successful pilot of electronic payments, but two years later another unit repeated the same early mistakes. What would most likely have prevented this? **Recording lessons learned and sharing them widely.**

flow: At the end of each project, hold a **lessons-learned meeting**: what worked, what did not, what we would do again
Write a short **lessons note** in a standard form, covering **failures** as well as successes
Store it in a place that all staff can find (an intranet library or project database)
Share it in a **community of practice**, newsletters and induction training
Check at the start of each new project whether earlier lessons apply

blocks.p: If two units in a ministry are each improving the same grant application process without knowing about the other, the director should **bring them together under one coordinated project**. A register of current improvement projects helps to avoid duplication.

Public services must remain open and fair to all. Before moving a service online only, consider citizens who have no internet access: keep a counter, a phone line or mobile service for them, and measure whether they are being left behind.

blocks.note: Public bodies in Jamaica are working to move more services online. Good managers count both the people who gain from the new route and the people who may be left out, and they follow the procurement and data protection rules in every project.
blocks.label: Jamaica

ul: explain the difference between innovation and continuous improvement, and why a public body needs both.

link an innovation programme to the corporate plan and explain risk appetite.

explain the procurement, data protection and fair-access checks needed for a new idea.
design a pilot with a baseline, measures and targets agreed in advance.

plan for different adopter groups and consult staff and their union early.

terms: Innovation
Bringing in something new that creates value, such as a new service, process or way of organising
Continuous improvement
Refining current ways of working in small, regular steps
Incremental innovation
A small improvement to an existing service or process
Radical innovation
A large change that replaces the old way of working
Risk appetite
The amount and type of risk a board is willing to accept in pursuit of its objectives
Open innovation
Using ideas from outside the organisation, such as universities, firms and citizens
Co-design
Designing a service together with the people who use it
Design thinking
A human-centred approach: understand users, define the problem, generate ideas, prototype and test
Prototype
An early, simple model of a service or tool that users can try and comment on
Stage-gate
A process with set stages and a go, change or stop decision between them
Business case
A document that sets out the problem, options, costs, benefits and risks to support a decision
Pilot
A small-scale trial of a new idea in one place before roll-out
Scaling up
Extending a proven innovation from a pilot site to the whole organisation
Early adopters / laggards
The early and the last groups to take up a new idea
PDCA
Plan, Do, Check, Act: the basic cycle of improvement
Lean
An approach that removes waste and speeds the flow of work
DMAIC
Define, Measure, Analyse, Improve, Control: the Six Sigma improvement cycle
Total quality management
An organisation-wide approach in which everyone works to improve quality, with the customer at the centre
Quality management system
The documented policies, processes and responsibilities used to manage quality
Benchmarking
Comparing your processes and results with those of the best similar organisations to learn from them
Community of practice
A group from different units who meet regularly to share methods and problems

c1.title: Choosing ideas at a municipal corporation in Clarendon
c1.text: The innovation committee of a municipal corporation in May Pen, Clarendon, has J$6,000,000 and three shortlisted ideas. The criteria and weights are impact 40%, cost 35% (a high score means low cost) and ease 25%, each scored out of 10. Idea P, a text-message reminder for market-stall fees, scores 8, 6 and 9. Idea Q, a mobile unit for building-plan advice in rural districts, scores 7, 5 and 6. Idea R, a new online payment portal for all fees, scores 9, 3 and 4 and would need a supplier that the corporation has not used before. The committee chair says the portal is the most exciting idea and wants it approved at once.

c2.title: Clinic reminders in St Elizabeth
c2.text: A regional health authority in St Elizabeth piloted text-message reminders at two rural clinics for three months. Before the pilot, 160 of 640 appointments (25%) were missed. During the pilot, 112 of 640 were missed. The pilot ran from December to February, when many people travel for the holidays and return to farm work. Some older patients do not have mobile phones. The authority's planning officer wants to roll the reminders out to every clinic in the region next month, and wants to share patients' phone numbers with a private text-messaging firm.

c3.title: Slow licence processing at an agency in Spanish Town
c3.text: A licensing agency in Spanish Town takes an average of 15 working days to issue a trade licence. A process map made by the staff shows that the officers' hands-on work takes about 45 minutes in total. The rest is waiting: files wait in trays for a signature, are carried between two buildings, and are often returned because of errors on the application form (about 1 in 10). The agency's director wants to improve the process and has asked the unit head, Mrs Hall, to lead the work. Mrs Hall is expected to be promoted to another post next year.

c4.title: Ideas going nowhere at a statutory body
c4.text: Staff at a statutory body in Kingston say that nothing happens to their ideas. The suggestion box is emptied once a year, any change needs sign-off from five separate committees, and last year one officer's trial of a new filing method failed and she was criticised in front of colleagues. Of 150 ideas received last year, 24 were put into practice. The chief executive wants more ideas and has asked for a plan to build a culture of innovation. The board has said it has a low appetite for risk to public safety but is open to new ways of serving customers.

c5.title: Moving a service online at a ministry
c5.text: A ministry plans to move its application for a small-business grant fully online. A university has offered to build the system for free if it can reuse the software. The ministry has two offices, each of which has started its own project to improve the grant forms, without telling the other. Officers in the parish offices, who deal with applicants without computers every day, were not asked their views. The new system would store applicants' ID numbers and business records.

questions.q: What is the weighted score of Idea P?
The chair wants the portal (Idea R) approved at once because it is exciting. What is the best response?
o: Score all ideas on the agreed criteria, then put the portal through a business case and gate
Approve the portal, because its highest impact score shows that it is the best idea overall
Reject the portal, because new ideas that need new suppliers are never worth the risk involved
Approve the portal and ask the supplier to prepare the business case for it afterwards
questions.why: Agreed criteria keep the choice fair, and a business case and gate decision protect public money. A high impact score alone does not show that the idea is good value.

questions.q: What must the corporation do before the portal is bought from a supplier it has not used before?
o: Ask the supplier to give the corporation a free trial for a full year
Get approval only from the committee chair, as the committee's head
Buy through the supplier the corporation used for its last project
Follow the procurement rules for public bodies
questions.why: Spending public money with a new supplier, even for a test, must follow the procurement rules for public bodies.

questions.q: The corporation's Idea P costs J$900,000 and is expected to save J$75,000 a month in collection costs. What is its simple payback period?
o: 9 months
12 months
15 months
75 months
questions.why: Payback = cost ÷ saving per month = 900,000 ÷ 75,000 = 12 months.

questions.q: By what percentage did missed appointments fall during the pilot?
questions.why: Missed appointments fell from 160 to 112, a drop of 48. (160 − 112) ÷ 160 × 100 = 30%. The fall in the rate is 25% to 17.5%, which is 7.5 percentage points, not 7.5%.

questions.q: Why should the authority be careful about the pilot result before rolling out?
o: A three-month pilot is never long enough to show any real effect at all
A fall in missed appointments is not a useful measure of success here
Rural clinics are always too different from urban clinics to be compared
The holiday season may have affected attendance, so other causes need checking
questions.why: Evaluate honestly by looking for other causes. Travel at holiday time may have changed attendance, so the authority should check against another period or a comparison clinic.

questions.q: What should the planning officer do about sharing patients' phone numbers with a private text-messaging firm?
o: Check the data protection law allows it, and agree what is shared and how it is secured
Share the numbers, because the firm is only sending messages to the clients for the authority
Share only the numbers of patients who attended the two pilot clinics in the trial
Share the numbers if the firm promises in a letter not to give them to anyone else
questions.why: Patient contact details are personal data. Sharing needs a lawful basis and clear controls on purpose and security, checked before the project goes ahead.

questions.q: Some older patients have no mobile phones. What should the authority do?
o: Continue with text messages only, since most of the patients do have mobile phones
Stop the pilot, since it does not work for everyone in the whole community
Keep other ways of reminding them, such as phone calls, and check their attendance
Ask older patients to buy a basic phone so that they can receive the messages
questions.why: Public services must stay open and fair to all. Keep or add other routes for those without phones and check that they are not left behind.

questions.q: Which kind of waste does the process map mainly show at the agency?
o: Over-production of licences that applicants have not asked for
Unused talent among the officers, who are bored with the work
Inventory of blank licence forms kept in the cabinets
Waiting, with transport and defects adding to the delay
questions.why: Out of 15 days, the hands-on work is 45 minutes, so almost all the time is waiting. Carrying files and sending back faulty forms add to it.

questions.q: Which approach focuses most directly on removing this kind of waste?
o: DMAIC alone, because it deals with accuracy and not with waiting
Lean
Benchmarking alone, because other agencies already have the answer
Total quality management alone, because it cannot be done by one unit
questions.why: Lean aims to remove waiting, hand-offs and unneeded steps. Six Sigma's DMAIC would help with the 1-in-10 error rate, and the two can be combined.

questions.q: About 1 in 10 applications is returned because of errors on the form. Which step best finds the cause?
o: Tell the applicants to be more careful when they fill in the form
Ask the officers to accept incomplete forms and fix them later themselves
Collect data on the errors, ask why five times and talk to applicants and staff
Add a second signature to every application before it is accepted
questions.why: Find the root cause with data and the people involved. Blaming applicants or adding a signature treats the symptom and adds more waiting.

questions.q: Mrs Hall may leave next year. What would best keep the gains after she moves?
o: Writing the new method into procedures, checklists and training
Asking her successor to read her handover notes at the end of the year
Asking the staff to remember the changes and to teach new officers
Presenting the results to the director once, at a final meeting
questions.why: Standardising the method in written procedures and training means it does not depend on one person.

questions.q: The suggestion box is emptied only once a year. What is the best change?
o: Name an officer to reply to every idea within a set time and publish what happens to it
Replace the box with one larger box that is emptied every second month by a clerk
Ask each director to choose the best idea from their own division at the end of the year
Tell staff that only ideas that save money will be read, to keep the workload down
questions.why: Quick replies and visible results show staff that ideas matter. Slow or silent systems make people stop sending them.

questions.q: What is the agency's implementation rate for last year's ideas?
questions.why: 24 ÷ 150 × 100 = 16%. (6.25% comes from dividing the wrong way round, 150 ÷ 24, and 84% is the share of ideas not used.)

questions.q: Which change would best deal with the five sign-off committees?
o: Add a sixth committee that checks whether the other five were right
A fast route for small tests, with clear authority delegated to a manager
Remove all sign-off so that staff can try anything they like
Keep the five committees and ask staff to be more patient
questions.why: Layered approval is a barrier. A faster route for low-risk tests, with delegated authority and controls, speeds learning while keeping public money safe.

questions.q: How should the chief executive treat the officer whose filing trial failed?
o: Speak to her privately and agree that she will not suggest any more trials
Put the failure in her appraisal as a rating of 2 for judgement
Say nothing, so that the matter is forgotten as soon as possible
Thank her, record what was learned and share it, and ask what support she needs
questions.why: A planned trial that fails still produces learning. Treating it that way encourages other staff to put forward ideas.

questions.q: Which simple tool would best help the ministry to avoid two units working on the same problem in future?
o: A rule that only one unit may propose projects each year
A register of current improvement projects that every unit can see
A monthly report from each unit on the hours its officers worked
An annual ceremony at which the best project is announced
questions.why: A shared register shows who is doing what, so units can join forces. The other options do not make project information visible.

questions.q: The university offers to build the system for free if it can reuse the software. What should the ministry do first?
o: Check the procurement rules and agree in writing who owns and may use the software and data
Accept at once, since a free offer from a university needs no formal approval at all
Accept if the university will promise not to reuse any of the ministry's own data
Decline, because universities should never work with public bodies on such systems
questions.why: Even a free offer can create obligations. Procurement rules apply, and the agreement should say who owns and may use the software and protect applicants' data.

questions.q: Which approach would best make use of the parish officers' knowledge in designing the new system?
o: Ask them to approve the finished system in a short email once it is complete
Train them after the launch, so that they can then help applicants to use it
Leave it to the university, since its technical staff know best how to build it
Co-design: involve the officers and some applicants in testing early versions
questions.why: Frontline staff and users know where processes fail. Co-design brings them in early, so the system fits real needs.

questions.q: The system will hold applicants' ID numbers and business records. Which step belongs in the plan before it goes live?
o: Ask applicants to agree that their records may be used for any purpose later
Store the records on a shared drive so that all ministries can read them
Agree who may see the records, how they are protected and how long they are kept
Leave data rules until after the first month, when problems have shown up
questions.why: Personal data must be protected from the start: who has access, how it is secured and how long it is kept are decided before launch, in line with the data protection law.
